blocks.text: On a Saturday in a ward in Ilorin, party agents in green, red or blue sit under the same mango tree, arguing over whose name will appear on the ballot. That argument is not a quarrel among friends: it is how a political party turns private ambition into a public choice, and how Nigerians decide who will occupy Aso Rock and the 469 seats of the National Assembly.

blocks.title: Political party
blocks.text: An organised group of people who share similar political ideas and seek to gain and exercise governmental power by contesting and winning elections. The aim of forming government is what distinguishes a party from a pressure group, a cultural association or a social club.

blocks.markdown: Section 221 of the **1999 Constitution** forbids any association other than a political party from canvassing for votes or contributing to a candidate. Parties must be registered with the **Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC)** and must have a national spread: their name, symbol and membership cannot be confined to a single ethnic, religious or regional group. That constitutional requirement is why Nigeria's registered parties present themselves as national organisations even when their strongest support is regional.

items: **Interest aggregation** — gathering the demands of different groups into a single programme that government can act on.
**Political recruitment** — selecting, training and presenting candidates for elective and appointive office.
**Political education and mobilisation** — explaining public issues and turning supporters out to register, campaign and vote.
**Manifesto and policy formulation** — publishing a programme of what the party will do if it wins power.
**Linkage** — connecting citizens to the state, so that grievances and hopes reach those who make law.
**Forming and running government** — organising a cabinet, defending policy and, if in opposition, offering an alternative government.
**Peaceful transfer of power** — providing a recognised channel through which one set of rulers can replace another without violence.

blocks.markdown:
### One-party, two-party and multi-party systems

A **party system** describes how many parties actually compete for, and have a realistic chance of winning, governmental power — not merely how many names appear on a register.

A **one-party system** allows only one legal party. Opposition is banned or absorbed. It produces clear direction and can mobilise a new state quickly, but it suppresses choice, encourages authoritarianism and makes peaceful change almost impossible. Historical examples include the USSR's Communist Party and Tanzania's TANU/CCM under Nyerere's early one-party constitution.

A **two-party system** is dominated by two large parties that alternate in office, even if smaller parties exist. The United States (Democrats and Republicans) is the standard example. It tends to produce stable majorities and a clear opposition, but it can squeeze out minority voices.

A **multi-party system** has three or more parties with a realistic chance of winning seats or joining a coalition. Most of continental Europe, and Nigeria's First, Second and Fourth Republics, are multi-party. It gives wider representation, but can produce unstable coalitions and ethnic or regional fragmentation.

blocks.markdown:
### Major parties of the Nigerian republics

**First Republic (1963–1966; party politics from 1960).** The three giants were regionally rooted:
- **NPC** (Northern People's Congress) — led by Sir Ahmadu Bello, the Sardauna of Sokoto; governed the Northern Region and, in alliance, the centre under Sir Abubakar Tafawa Balewa.
- **NCNC** (National Council of Nigeria and the Cameroons, later National Council of Nigerian Citizens) — founded 1944 with Herbert Macaulay as president and Nnamdi Azikiwe as secretary; strongest in the East.
- **AG** (Action Group) — founded 1951 by Chief Obafemi Awolowo from the Egbe Omo Oduduwa; strongest in the West; manifesto of free education and welfarism.

**Second Republic (1979–1983).** Five parties were registered. The three that matter most for examinations are the **NPN** (National Party of Nigeria, which produced President Shehu Shagari), the **UPN** (Unity Party of Nigeria, Awolowo) and the **NPP** (Nigerian People's Party, Azikiwe). The GNPP and PRP completed the five.

**Third Republic (aborted 1993).** A legally imposed two-party system: the **Social Democratic Party (SDP)** and the **National Republican Convention (NRC)**.

**Fourth Republic (1999–).** The **People's Democratic Party (PDP)**, formed in 1998, governed from 1999 to 2015. The **All Progressives Congress (APC)** was formed in 2013 from a merger of the ACN, CPC, ANPP and a faction of APGA, and won the presidency in 2015. Other registered parties exist, but PDP and APC have been the two dominant competitors.

blocks.title: Classifying Nigeria's party systems by republic
blocks.prompt: A WAEC essay asks: 'Identify the party system operated in each Nigerian republic and name two major parties in each case.' Plan a four-part answer.

steps.text: Define the terms first. A multi-party system has three or more parties able to win power; a two-party system is dominated by two; a one-party system legalises only one. Nigeria has never run a one-party republic.
First Republic: multi-party. Evidence: NPC, NCNC and AG all held regional governments and contested the centre. Name NPC and NCNC, or NPC and AG.
Second Republic: multi-party. Five parties were registered; NPN, UPN and NPP were the principal ones. Name NPN and UPN.
Third Republic: two-party by law, not by voter choice. IBB registered only SDP and NRC. Name both, and note that the June 1993 election was annulled, so the republic was aborted.

Fourth Republic: multi-party in law and in the register, with two dominant parties in practice — PDP and APC. Examiners still credit it as multi-party because other parties contest and occasionally win seats.
Close with a caution: do not call the Fourth Republic a two-party system just because APC and PDP dominate. Dominance is not the same as a legal two-party arrangement.

blocks.answer: First Republic multi-party (NPC, NCNC, AG); Second Republic multi-party (NPN, UPN, NPP); aborted Third Republic two-party (SDP, NRC); Fourth Republic multi-party, dominated in practice by PDP and APC

blocks.title: Do not confuse party with party system
blocks.text: A common lost mark is writing that Nigeria 'has a two-party system because of APC and PDP'. A party system is a legal and practical arrangement, not a headcount of the two biggest names. The Fourth Republic is multi-party; only the aborted Third Republic was a two-party system by decree. Also learn the initials in full: NPC, NCNC, AG, NPN, UPN, NPP, PDP, APC.

points: A political party is an organised group that seeks to form government by contesting elections, unlike a pressure group which only tries to influence those already in power.

Its functions include interest aggregation, recruitment of leaders, political education, publishing a manifesto, linking citizens to the state, forming government or opposition, and making peaceful change of rulers possible.
A one-party system legalises only one party; a two-party system is dominated by two; a multi-party system has three or more with a realistic chance of winning power.
Nigeria's First, Second and Fourth Republics have been multi-party; the aborted Third Republic was a legally imposed two-party system of SDP and NRC.
First Republic giants: NPC, NCNC and AG. Second Republic: NPN, UPN and NPP. Fourth Republic: PDP (1998) and APC (2013).
